Mark Twain (born Samuel Langhorne Clemens, November 30, 1835 - April 21, 1910) was an American writer, humorist, and essayist. He was praised as the "greatest humorist the United States has produced," with William Faulkner calling him "the father of American literature."

Famous Books:

  • The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876)
  • Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884)
  • A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889)
  • The Prince and the Pauper (1881)
  • Life on the Mississippi (1883)

Mark Twain (born Samuel Langhorne Clemens, November 30, 1835 - April 21, 1910) was an American writer, humorist, and essayist. He was praised as the "greatest humorist the United States has produced," with William Faulkner calling him "the father of American literature."

Famous Books:

  • The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876)
  • Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884)
  • A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889)
  • The Prince and the Pauper (1881)
  • Life on the Mississippi (1883)

Alexandre Dumas (24 July 1802 – 5 December 1870), also known as Alexandre Dumas père, was a French novelist and playwright. His works have been translated into nearly 100 languages and he is one of the most widely read French authors.

Famous Books:

  • The Three Musketeers (1844)
  • The Count of Monte Cristo (1844)
  • Twenty Years After (1845)
  • The Vicomte of Bragelonne (1847)

Charles Dickens (7 February 1812 – 9 June 1870) was an English writer and social critic. He created some of the world's best-known fictional characters and is regarded as the greatest novelist of the Victorian era.

Famous Books:

  • Oliver Twist (1837)
  • A Christmas Carol (1843)
  • David Copperfield (1849)
  • A Tale of Two Cities (1859)
  • Great Expectations (1860)

Victor Hugo (26 February 1802 – 22 May 1885) was a French Romantic writer, poet, and politician. He is considered one of the greatest and best-known French writers.

Famous Books:

  • The Hunchback of Notre-Dame (1831)
  • Les Misérables (1862)
  • The Man Who Laughs (1869)
  • Toilers of the Sea (1866)

Isaac Asimov (January 2, 1920 – April 6, 1992) was an American writer and professor of biochemistry. He was known for his works of science fiction and popular science.

Famous Books:

  • Foundation (1951)
  • I, Robot (1950)
  • The Caves of Steel (1953)
  • The Gods Themselves (1972)

J.R.R. Tolkien (3 January 1892 – 2 September 1973) was an English writer, poet, and academic professor at Oxford University. He is best known for his classic high fantasy works.

Famous Books:

  • The Hobbit (1937)
  • The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (1954)
  • The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers (1954)
  • The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (1955)

J.K. Rowling (born 31 July 1965) is a British author and philanthropist. She is best known for writing the Harry Potter fantasy series, which has sold more than 500 million copies.

Famous Books:

  • Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone (1997)
  • Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (1998)
  • Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (1999)
  • Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2000)
  • Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (2003)
  • Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (2005)
  • Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (2007)

Arthur C. Clarke (16 December 1917 – 19 March 2008) was a British science fiction writer, futurist, and inventor. He co-wrote the screenplay for the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

Famous Books:

  • Childhood's End (1953)
  • 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968)
  • Rendezvous with Rama (1973)
  • The Fountains of Paradise (1979)

Homer (c. 8th century BC) was an ancient Greek poet who is credited as the author of the Iliad and the Odyssey. Homer is considered one of the most revered and influential authors in history.

Famous Books:

  • The Iliad (c. 8th century BC)
  • The Odyssey (c. 8th century BC)

Note: Exact birth and death dates are unknown. Homer lived approximately in the 8th century BC.

William Shakespeare (23 April 1564 – 23 April 1616) was an English playwright, poet, and actor. He is widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language.

Famous Works:

  • Romeo and Juliet (1595)
  • Hamlet (1599)
  • Macbeth (1605)
  • Othello (1603)
  • King Lear (1605)
  • Sonnet 18 (1609)

Leo Tolstoy (9 September 1828 – 20 November 1910) was a Russian writer who is regarded as one of the greatest authors of all time.

Famous Books:

  • War and Peace (1869)
  • Anna Karenina (1878)
  • The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886)
  • Resurrection (1899)

Fyodor Dostoevsky (11 November 1821 – 9 February 1881) was a Russian novelist, short story writer, and journalist. His literary works explore human psychology in 19th-century Russia.

Famous Books:

  • Crime and Punishment (1866)
  • The Idiot (1869)
  • Demons (1872)
  • The Brothers Karamazov (1880)

Ernest Hemingway (July 21, 1899 – July 2, 1961) was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist. His economical and understated style had a strong influence on 20th-century fiction.

Famous Books:

  • The Old Man and the Sea (1952)
  • A Farewell to Arms (1929)
  • For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940)
  • The Sun Also Rises (1926)

Ferdowsi (c. 935 – c. 1025) was a Persian poet and the author of Shahnameh ("Book of Kings"), which is the world's longest epic poem created by a single poet.

Famous Books:

  • Shahnameh (Book of Kings) (1010)

Edgar Allan Poe (January 19, 1809 – October 7, 1849) was an American writer, poet, editor, and literary critic. He is best known for his tales of mystery and the macabre.

Famous Works:

  • The Raven (1845) - poem
  • The Tell-Tale Heart (1843) - short story
  • The Fall of the House of Usher (1839)
  • The Murders in the Rue Morgue (1841)

Jane Austen (16 December 1775 – 18 July 1817) was an English novelist known primarily for her six major novels, which critique the British landed gentry.

Famous Books:

  • Pride and Prejudice (1813)
  • Sense and Sensibility (1811)
  • Emma (1815)
  • Mansfield Park (1814)
  • Persuasion (1817)

Frederick Forsyth (born 25 August 1938) is an English novelist and journalist. He is best known for his thrillers. His books have sold more than 70 million copies worldwide.

Famous Books:

  • The Day of the Jackal (1971)
  • The Odessa File (1972)
  • The Dogs of War (1974)
  • The Fourth Protocol (1984)

John Grisham (born February 8, 1955) is an American novelist, lawyer, and former politician. He is best known for his popular legal thrillers. His books have been translated into 42 languages.

Famous Books:

  • A Time to Kill (1989)
  • The Firm (1991)
  • The Pelican Brief (1992)
  • The Client (1993)
  • The Rainmaker (1995)

Lee Child (born 29 October 1954) is a British author. He is the author of the Jack Reacher series of thriller novels. The series has sold over 100 million copies worldwide.

Famous Books (Jack Reacher Series):

  • Killing Floor (1997)
  • Die Trying (1998)
  • Tripwire (1999)
  • Echo Burning (2001)
  • Without Fail (2002)
  • Persuader (2003)
  • One Shot (2005)

Michel Zévaco (1 February 1860 – 8 August 1918) was a French journalist, novelist, and publisher. He is best known for his swashbuckling novels, particularly the Pardaillan series.

Famous Books (Pardaillan Series):

  • The Pardaillan (1900)
  • The Heroic Pardaillan (1901)
  • The Epic of the Pardaillan (1902)
  • The Pardaillan Captain (1905)
  • The Chevalier of Pardaillan (1907)

The Adventures of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain is an 1876 novel about a young boy growing up along the Mississippi River. The story is set in the fictional town of St. Petersburg, inspired by Hannibal, Missouri, where Twain lived.

The novel follows the mischievous Tom Sawyer, his friend Huckleberry Finn, and their adventures including witnessing a murder, becoming pirates, finding treasure, and getting lost in a cave. It is considered one of the greatest classics of American literature.

Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is a novel by Mark Twain, first published in 1884. It is a direct sequel to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and is often considered the "Great American Novel."

The book tells the story of Huck Finn and his journey down the Mississippi River with an escaped slave named Jim. It explores themes of race, identity, and morality in pre-Civil War America.

The Three Musketeers is a historical adventure novel written by Alexandre Dumas, first published in 1844. It is set in the 17th century and follows the adventures of a young man named d'Artagnan who joins the three musketeers of the King: Athos, Porthos, and Aramis.

The novel is famous for the slogan "All for one, one for all" and has been adapted into numerous films, television series, and stage productions.

The Count of Monte Cristo is an adventure novel by Alexandre Dumas, published in 1844. It is often considered one of Dumas's greatest works, alongside The Three Musketeers.

The story follows Edmond Dantès, who is falsely imprisoned in the Château d'If. After escaping, he acquires a fortune and seeks revenge on those who wronged him, transforming into the mysterious Count of Monte Cristo.

Oliver Twist is the second novel by Charles Dickens, published as a serial from 1837 to 1839. It tells the story of an orphan boy who escapes from a workhouse to London.

In London, Oliver falls in with a group of juvenile pickpockets led by the elderly criminal Fagin. The novel exposes the harsh realities of poverty and child labor in Victorian England.

A Tale of Two Cities is a historical novel by Charles Dickens, published in 1859. It is set in London and Paris before and during the French Revolution.

The novel tells the story of Dr. Manette, his daughter Lucie, and her husband Charles Darnay, a French aristocrat. It explores themes of resurrection, sacrifice, and social injustice.

Great Expectations is the thirteenth novel by Charles Dickens, published in 1861. It is considered one of his greatest and most sophisticated works.

The novel follows the story of Pip, an orphan boy who rises from humble beginnings to become a gentleman, thanks to a mysterious benefactor. It explores themes of social class, ambition, and moral redemption.

Les Misérables is a French historical novel by Victor Hugo, first published in 1862. It is considered one of the greatest novels of the 19th century.

The story follows Jean Valjean, a former convict who seeks redemption while being pursued by the ruthless Inspector Javert. Set against the backdrop of revolutionary France, the novel explores themes of justice, love, and sacrifice.

The Hunchback of Notre-Dame is a French Gothic novel by Victor Hugo, published in 1831. The story is set in Paris during the reign of Louis XI.

The novel focuses on the tragic story of Quasimodo, the deformed bell-ringer of Notre-Dame Cathedral, and his love for the beautiful Romani dancer Esmeralda.

Foundation is the first novel in Isaac Asimov's Foundation series, published in 1951. It is considered a landmark in science fiction literature.

The story follows a group of scientists who create a foundation to preserve knowledge and shorten the coming dark ages after the fall of the Galactic Empire.

I, Robot is a collection of nine science fiction short stories by Isaac Asimov, first published in 1950. It introduced the famous Three Laws of Robotics.

The stories explore the interaction between humans and robots, examining the moral and ethical implications of artificial intelligence.

The Hobbit, or There and Back Again, is a children's fantasy novel by J.R.R. Tolkien, published in 1937. It serves as a prelude to The Lord of the Rings.

The story follows Bilbo Baggins, a hobbit who is recruited by the wizard Gandalf to join a group of dwarves on a quest to reclaim their homeland from the dragon Smaug.
The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring

The Fellowship of the Ring is the first volume of J.R.R. Tolkien's epic fantasy novel The Lord of the Rings, published in 1954. It is widely considered one of the greatest works of fantasy literature.

The story follows Frodo Baggins as he sets out from the Shire to destroy the One Ring, accompanied by the Fellowship of the Ring.
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is the first novel in the Harry Potter series by J.K. Rowling, published in 1997. It introduces the young wizard Harry Potter.

The story follows Harry as he discovers his magical heritage, attends Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, and faces the dark wizard Lord Voldemort.

2001: A Space Odyssey is a science fiction novel by Arthur C. Clarke, published in 1968. It was developed concurrently with the film of the same name directed by Stanley Kubrick.

The novel follows a voyage to Jupiter with the sentient computer HAL 9000, exploring themes of evolution, technology, and extraterrestrial life.

The Iliad is an ancient Greek epic poem attributed to Homer, dating to the 8th century BC. It is one of the oldest works of Western literature.

The poem describes the events of the Trojan War, focusing on the hero Achilles and his quarrel with King Agamemnon.

The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic poem attributed to Homer, dating to the 8th century BC. It is a sequel to the Iliad and one of the foundational works of Western literature.

The poem follows the hero Odysseus on his ten-year journey home after the Trojan War, facing monsters, gods, and other obstacles.

Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare early in his career, first published in 1597. It is one of his most famous plays.

The play tells the story of two young star-crossed lovers whose deaths ultimately reconcile their feuding families.

The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, often shortened to Hamlet, is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written between 1599 and 1601. It is Shakespeare's longest play and one of his most quoted works.

The play dramatizes Prince Hamlet's revenge against his uncle Claudius, who has murdered Hamlet's father and married his mother.

War and Peace is a literary masterpiece by Leo Tolstoy, first published in 1869. It is considered one of the greatest novels ever written.

The novel chronicles the French invasion of Russia and its impact on several aristocratic families, exploring themes of history, fate, and human nature.

Anna Karenina is a novel by Leo Tolstoy, published in 1878. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest works of literature ever written.

The novel explores themes of love, betrayal, and social change through the tragic story of Anna Karenina and her affair with Count Vronsky.

Crime and Punishment is a novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, first published in 1866. It is considered one of the greatest novels of all time.

The story follows Rodion Raskolnikov, a former student who plans and commits murder, and his subsequent psychological and moral struggles.

The Brothers Karamazov is the final novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, published in 1880. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest achievements in world literature.

The novel explores deep philosophical themes of God, free will, and morality through the story of the three Karamazov brothers.
The Old Man and the Sea

The Old Man and the Sea is a short novel by Ernest Hemingway, published in 1952. It was the last major work of fiction published during his lifetime and won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1953.

The story follows an aging Cuban fisherman Santiago and his epic struggle to catch a giant marlin in the Gulf Stream.

The Shahnameh is an epic poem written by the Persian poet Ferdowsi, completed in 1010 AD. It is the world's longest epic poem created by a single author.

The poem tells the mythical and historical past of Greater Iran, containing 50,000 couplets and exploring themes of kingship, heroism, and the battle between good and evil.

The Raven is a narrative poem by Edgar Allan Poe, first published in 1845. It is one of the most famous poems in American literature.

The poem tells the story of a distraught lover who is visited by a mysterious raven that can only say "Nevermore." The collection includes other famous works like "The Tell-Tale Heart" and "The Fall of the House of Usher."

Pride and Prejudice is a romantic novel by Jane Austen, first published in 1813. It is one of the most beloved novels in English literature.

The story follows the character Elizabeth Bennet as she deals with issues of manners, upbringing, morality, education, and marriage in the society of the landed gentry of early 19th-century England.

The Day of the Jackal is a thriller novel by Frederick Forsyth, published in 1971. It was his debut novel and won the Edgar Award for Best Novel.

The story follows a professional assassin known as the "Jackal" who is hired to assassinate French President Charles de Gaulle.

The Firm is a legal thriller by John Grisham, published in 1991. It was his second novel and became a bestseller, adapted into a 1993 film starring Tom Cruise.

The story follows a young lawyer who joins a small but prosperous law firm, only to discover that it is involved in illegal activities.

Killing Floor is the debut novel by Lee Child, published in 1997. It introduces the character Jack Reacher, a former military policeman and drifter.

The story follows Reacher as he arrives in the small town of Margrave, Georgia, where he is arrested for murder and must clear his name while uncovering a larger conspiracy.

Pardaillan is a swashbuckling adventure novel by Michel Zévaco, first published in 1900. It is the first book in the Pardaillan series.

The novel follows the adventures of the heroic knight Pardaillan during the French Wars of Religion in the 16th century.
